metadata.description: A first-class allocatable range of IP addresses that Network.IPAddress records are carved from — the DHCP subnet pool (RFC 2131 subnet4 pools/ranges) as its own record, so allocation OWNERSHIP is expressible: which addresses are in play, which tenant/resource holds each, and whether the pool is exhausted. Same allocatable-pool pattern as Storage.Pool→Storage.Dataset (a pool is the source; the carved record depends_on it). Distinct from Network.DHCPScope (the SERVICE-side subnet config a DHCP provider realizes) and Network.IPAddress (a single CONSUMED address): the Pool is the intent-side inventory the addresses are allocated FROM.

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

prefix.description: The subnet the pool draws from, as CIDR (RFC 8344), e.g. 192.0.2.0/24.

ranges.description: The allocatable ranges within the prefix (RFC 2131 subnet4 pools). Absent = the whole prefix minus exclusions is allocatable.

allocation_mode.description: How addresses leave the pool: dynamic = leased on request (DHCP), static = fixed reservations bound ahead of time, mixed = both. Aligns with Network.IPAddress.allocation on the carved record.

exclusions.description: Addresses withheld from allocation (gateway, broadcast, known-static, avoid-buggy). Not carved even if inside a range.

total_addresses.description: DERIVED — computed from the pool's declared ranges (compute-never-store; a stored copy could disagree with the arithmetic). Count of allocatable addresses (ranges minus exclusions), once Realized.

allocated_count.description: DERIVED — a count of the Network.IPAddress records allocated_from this pool; those records are the source (compute-never-store). Addresses currently allocated from this pool.

free_count.description: DERIVED — total_addresses minus allocated_count, both themselves derived; never stored independently. Remaining allocatable addresses.

exhausted.description: True when free_count == 0 — the pool-exhaustion signal capacity/placement and quota policies read.

relationships.name: subnet
relationships.description: The L3 network these ranges carve up. Added 2026-08-10 with Network.Subnet: a pool is an ALLOCATION surface (which addresses may be handed out), never the network itself (what the network is, where its gateway is). Before the subnet class existed this pool's own `prefix` was standing in for both, which conflated the two.

relationships.name: network
relationships.description: The network segment this pool serves. A pool is scoped to one L2/L3 segment (VirtualNetwork/VLAN); addresses carved from it are reachable on that segment.

adopts.role: allocatable-range shape: a pool is one or more contiguous address ranges within a subnet from which addresses are handed out (dynamic) or reserved (static)
prefix + ip_family shape reused from Network.IPAddress (same family, ADR-023)

context.purpose: Makes an allocatable IP range a first-class record so allocation ownership and exhaustion are visible facts.
context.plain_description: A range of addresses that individual address records are carved from: the required subnet `prefix` (CIDR), the allocatable `ranges` inside it (start/end pairs — this allocation-side name differs from a DHCP scope's `pools` by design), `exclusions` (gateway, broadcast, known statics), and how addresses leave it — `allocation_mode`: `dynamic` (leased), `static` (reserved ahead of time), or `mixed`. Once realized it reports totals — allocated, free, exhausted — the signal capacity and placement policies read before asking for another address. Same pattern as a storage pool feeding datasets: the pool is the source, the carved record depends on it.
use_when: You need to know which addresses are in play, who holds each, and when a range is close to exhausted.
You need address allocation scoped to the one network segment the pool serves.
not_for: Service-side DHCP config for the subnet (options, lease time) — Network.DHCPScope; the pool is intent-side inventory. The range overlap between the two is deliberate and documented on both.
A single address — Network.IPAddress, carved from this pool.
works_with: Network.IPAddress — the records carved from the pool (allocated_from).
Network.VirtualNetwork — the segment the pool serves.
Network.DHCPScope — the service-side projection of the same subnet.
